articles.title: FX Daily: Defensive rotation in play
articles.author: Chris Turner, Frantisek Taborsky, Francesco Pesole
articles.fulltext:
It looks like markets are going through a subtle regime shift. Higher energy prices no longer mean higher rates forever; instead, the long end is starting to express a little more fear about growth. The upcoming US midterms may also be playing a role. It looks like there is some defensive rotation underway into the Swiss franc, the yen and sterling
USD: Midterms could be starting to play a role
Risk assets are on the back foot this European morning as energy prices stay firm and tech stocks remain fragile. On the former, a hefty risk premium remains in oil prices as attacks against Saudi Arabia continue. On the latter, Q3 results from Meta and Tesla and what they mean for capex plans are still being digested, but there clearly remains a fine line to walk. The suspicion now is that global equity investors are starting to scale back their exposure to the tech sector and looking for more defensive plays in sectors like consumer staples, healthcare and utilities. This will favour more geographic allocation to European equities, where tech weights in benchmark indices are lower. The upcoming US midterms in early November may also play a role here, where a Democrat sweep of Congress could slow/reverse deregulation.
At the same time, we are seeing a subtle change in the rate markets. During the late summer and especially in September, higher energy prices were associated with 'higher rates forever'. The one-month USD OIS priced 10 years forward traded at 5.17% – miles away from any neutral rate near 3.50%. These views are now changing. That OIS pricing has now dropped back to 4.85% as yield curves have flattened and investors seem to be a little more worried about growth than inflation.
This environment probably favours a little more outperformance of the defensive currencies over commodity currencies. But until the rock-solid short-end of the US yield curve starts to buckle, it is hard to make the case that the dollar needs to fall across the board.
We favour consolidation over correction for the DXY dollar index, but do not rule out some further softening to the 101.25/30 area.
The US data calendar is light again and we expect the dollar to be dragged around by tech stocks.
Chris Turner
EUR: Hard to be constructive
EUR/USD is trading quite well despite higher energy prices and an unresolved French budget crisis. One can only conclude that the biggest market driver at the moment is the heavy and concentrated positioning in US tech and the dollar, which is being gently pared back. Expect FX traders to keep a very close watch on the short end of the US curve now. Expectations for further Fed tightening have stayed rock-solid at around +75bp over recent weeks. We think that could remain the case for the coming months and that the dollar could stay strong. But any tech wobble that prompts a dovish re-pricing at the short-end could lead to a broader dollar correction.
There is little on the eurozone calendar today apart from the last of the ECB speakers before the blackout period commences later today. See here for a preview of next week's ECB meeting .
We do not think there is a strong case for EUR/USD to trade a lot higher. But if US tech does suffer now, a break of 1.1270/75 could open up 1.1340/50. However, we would not chase the rally. 1.13 remains our one-month forecast as outlined in this month's FX Talking.
Chris Turner
GBP: Back in fashion
It seems like sterling is riding on the coat-tails of PM Andy Burnham's popularity. In reality, it looks like there is both independent sterling strength and independent euro weakness at play in EUR/GBP. Earlier this summer, we had felt that sterling gains would not last. But now greater market confidence in a Bank of England tightening cycle – we look for 25bp hikes in February and November – makes sterling a high-carry European currency.
Next week's UK budget looks unlikely to derail the recent EUR/GBP break below 0.8400. And with the euro still having plenty of room to drop on French politics, EUR/GBP can stay offered in a 0.8360-0,8430 range for the time being.
Chris Turner
TRY: Easing resumes as carry trade holds
We expect the Central Bank of Turkey to resume its easing cycle for the first time since the US-Iran conflict began today, cutting rates by 100bp to 36.00%. September’s inflation data provided a positive signal, while developments in investment funds point to downside risks for the economy in the final quarter. The authorities’ swift response appears to have contained the fund shock, with no signs of systemic risk or a sharp rise in dollarisation, while foreign inflows have resumed.
However, it may further weaken domestic demand through tighter liquidity, wealth losses and lower confidence. Repayments to smaller investors could cushion consumption, but counterparty exposures remain the main spillover risk. Inflation sentiment has improved after benign September data and expectations of weaker demand. We expect 100bp cuts in October and December, taking the policy rate to 35% by year-end, versus our 29.0% inflation forecast for year-end.
Although crowded long TRY positions offer less and less carry, they remain popular in emerging markets, and we expect this demand to persist in the coming months despite renewed rate cuts. The recent weekly adjustment in USD/TRY does not alter the overall FX setup, and the carry trade continues. We expect a level of 51.50 USD/TRY by the end of the year.
Frantisek Taborsky

articles.title: FX Daily: Dollar shows fresh vulnerability to oil price drops
articles.author: Francesco Pesole, Frantisek Taborsky, Chris Turner
articles.fulltext:
Some lingering AI concerns appear to have left the dollar in a more fragile position overall. Yesterday, the greenback briefly dipped on some tentative news about progress in the Middle East. Further drops in oil prices now show greater potential to harm the USD. France remains in focus for the euro, with EUR/CHF still facing downside risks
USD: Softer momentum continues
The dollar continues to trade with a soft undertone. That, to us, is a mix of some aftereffects of AI-related concerns (CoreWeave bonds had another wobble yesterday) and stretched longs/ short-term overvaluations being unwound. That said, the dollar no longer looks particularly stretched on our short-term valuation metrics. Across the G10, GBP, NOK and AUD are trading slightly rich versus the USD. CAD and CHF are broadly at fair value, while EUR, JPY, SEK and NZD remain undervalued. Importantly, all sit within the 1.5 standard deviation band, leaving little in the way of strong valuation signals.
Yesterday, there was also a reminder that lower oil prices can damage the dollar. A short-lived drop in Brent on unconfirmed reports of Middle East negotiation progress was enough to send DXY briefly to 101.50. With the supply picture improving, elevated oil prices are relying increasingly on geopolitical risk. FX markets may therefore start to price in a sharp decline in crude if signs of genuine progress emerge.
And the dollar’s reaction function to oil may have changed over the past week or so. Rising concerns about tech stocks have somewhat dented the market’s hawkish conviction on the Fed, allowing for greater dovish flexibility at the front end in response to non-data inputs like an oil selloff.
We recognise that the softer dollar backdrop has shifted the balance of risks somewhat further in a USD-bearish direction. Even so, we continue to favour a gradual and orderly dollar decline rather than a sharper depreciation. The broader Fed, oil and rates narrative remains supportive.
The US calendar is quiet today. Yesterday’s surprise drop in housing starts reinforced the notion of a deteriorating real estate market. Attention will instead centre on any follow-up headlines pointing to progress in US-Iran negotiations today.
Francesco Pesole
EUR: French spreads widen further
French bonds sold off again yesterday, with the 10yr OAT-Bund spread widening to 157bp at one point, close to the 159bp 2 October high. Lingering concerns about the budget are clearly being compounded by rising social unrest. Our France economist discusses here the potential economic implications of the riots. And on Friday there is a looming Moody’s rating review of France, which could keep sentiment on OATs soft.
With EUR/USD affected by softish USD momentum, EUR/CHF remains the clearer exhaust valve of French risk into FX. Yesterday saw another attempted break lower, with support emerging again around 0.9230, close to the 200-day MA. A break below that level could prompt a gap to below 0.920. Risks remain on the downside there. In EUR/USD, we could see some further consolidation at 1.120-1.125.
EUR/GBP also continues to show intense selling pressure, having broken below 0.840. While French risk is playing a role, the pound is emerging as an outperformer in G10. Markets are sinking their teeth into a positive UK growth story and BoE tightening alongside expectations that next week’s budget won’t deliver any real surprises ( here’s what could go wrong ).
This morning, UK headline inflation for September came in slightly hotter than expected at 3.5%. Services CPI also beat expectations with an acceleration to 3.7%, but was probably exaggerated by airfares. By our calculations , 'energy intensive' inflation is still showing no signs of picking up and is in fact lower than it was earlier this year. Food prices fell on the month, capping a remarkably benign period of supermarket inflation. In short, still no sign of second-round effects in these numbers.
While a November hike by the BoE appears likely now, expectations for 100bp worth of tightening by June remain way too hawkish in our view. The pound’s rally is looking stretched by short-term valuation metrics, and we see growing risks of corrections, both vs EUR and USD.
Francesco Pesole
NZD: Barring an inflation surprise, RBNZ should hike next week
New Zealand releases important 3Q CPI figures overnight. We expect the headline to slow from 4.1% to 3.8%, in line with consensus and marginally below the RBNZ’s 3.9% projection. Any, even small, upside surprise will, in our view, consolidate expectations of an October hike further.
Markets have been pricing around 18-21bp for next week’s meeting since RBNZ’s Chief Economist Paul Conway delivered hawkish remarks last week. He explicitly said this month’s decision is wide open, that he sees risk to the upside for 4Q CPI and that the NZD weakness is worrying. It felt like an attempt to drive market pricing higher, and barring a major surprise lower in CPI tomorrow, we expect a 25bp hike next week.
NZD remains cheap relative to its short-term fair value model, and we expect it to keep recovering ground against its closest peer, AUD. We see NZD/USD trading above 0.570 into year-end.
Francesco Pesole
HUF: Improving domestic outlook meets global headwinds
Yesterday, Hungary unveiled a full fiscal path plan, under which the deficit is projected to decline from 4.9% next year to 2.8% by 2030. According to the prime minister, Hungary aims to adopt the euro as soon as possible. The National Bank of Hungary kept interest rates unchanged at 5.50% yesterday and reiterated previous statements regarding euro adoption, noting that the fiscal path aligns with the euro adoption plan. At the same time, the governor pointed out that rising core yields, uncertainty, and inflationary risks necessitate a cautious monetary policy.
In our view, this accurately captures the current situation: while the domestic narrative is evolving positively – to the market's satisfaction – the global environment remains unfavourable. Our economists see a possibility of a rate cut toward the end of the year, provided that the global situation, particularly energy prices, stabilises.
Following the release of the budget plan for next year on Monday, the market is undergoing a correction after a rally in previous weeks. As we have discussed, long positions on Hungary had become overly crowded; the "buy the rumour, sell the fact" scenario has fully played out, and we are likely to see further profit-taking. Nevertheless, as we noted in recent days, the domestic story is moving in the right direction, and we believe the market will soon take advantage of lower price levels to re-enter new positions.
EUR/HUF has experienced some upward pressure, tracking movements in rates and bonds. However, positioning is likely not overly crowded as in fixed income, and the NBH is not currently signalling imminent rate cuts, which should keep the exchange rate anchored. Over the past two weeks, EUR/HUF has remained within a tight range of 362-364, and its next direction will likely depend more on global developments. Yesterday’s signs of a potential easing of tensions between the US and Iran could provide a positive boost, helping the pair move toward the lower end of its current range.
Frantisek Taborsky

articles.title: Rates Spark: France still singled out
articles.author: Benjamin Schroeder
articles.fulltext:
Revived diplomatic efforts around the Middle East lift market sentiment, but French spreads still widened beyond 150bp. Fiscal concerns and public unrest clearly weigh on French government bonds (OATs), but more is at play
France remains singled out, but it's not pure credit concerns
Risk sentiment was more upbeat after headlines suggesting a revival of diplomatic efforts to end the Middle East conflict. Energy prices retreated from their recent highs, stocks advanced, and yields edged lower. Still, markets have learnt to treat such headlines with a healthy dose of scepticism.
Within the European government bond space, a tentative stabilisation of spreads over Bunds mirrored the improved sentiment. However, France continues to be singled out, with the 10y spread pushing past 150bp. We had cautioned that the public unrest was adding to concerns around France's ability to consolidate its finances. The unrest also adds very direct costs in terms of lost GDP , as our economist warns.
Back during the days of the sovereign debt crisis, the French spread versus Germany peaked at just below 200bp. But bear in mind, this was when Italian spreads pushed past 500bp and markets were contemplating the tail risk of a collapsing monetary union, i.e., redenomination risk.
To add some perspective, a 10y spread of close to 200bp in late 2011 meant that French bonds yielded more than twice as much as German Bunds. The 10y Bund yield stood at around 1.9%. Nowadays, French 10y bonds, at just below 5%, yield less than 1.5 times as much as their German counterpart. And that 5% mark in outright yields appears to remain a hurdle for OATs for now.
This is not to say that spreads cannot push further, especially in the absence of any good news and with a long way to go until the presidential elections. But it is important to highlight that there are other factors pushing spreads wider that do not directly reflect pure credit concerns. Overall, rates volatility has increased and weighs on spreads more generally. Especially when market liquidity is subdued, this can exacerbate widening pressures across EGBs. The French CDS spread, for that matter, while wider, is still 160bp away from its 2011 peaks rather than a bit over 40bp when looking at the bond spread.
Wednesday’s events and market view
Following the UK CPI release in the morning, it will be a quiet day in terms of data. The main focus will be the public appearances of BoE Governor Bailey and ECB President Lagarde.
In the primary government bond markets, the US will auction 20y bonds (US$13bn). The European primary is quiet. Italy’s two retail BTP Valore bonds are still open for subscription through the week.

articles.title: FX Daily: AI jitters have damaged USD safe haven appeal
articles.author: Francesco Pesole, Frantisek Taborsky
articles.fulltext:
After big moves in front-end USD rates, the dollar has shown it could be a laggard in further stock market instability if led by AI concerns. Still, we don’t think we are on the brink of a major USD decline. EUR/USD may struggle to stay supported today as protests in France spill over into local assets, while we see limited impact from US-Ukraine news for now
USD: AI jitters leave USD on less solid ground
AI-related jitters entered the FX picture last week, although currencies are more accurately borrowing the reaction from the rates channel. The USD two-year OIS/SOFR has dropped 25bp from the 14 October post-US CPI print. These are mammoth moves considering they have been driven almost entirely by AI concerns, with effectively no macro input.
Markets appear to have a clear reaction function in mind: stock market turmoil is enough to drastically reduce Federal Reserve tightening plans, even with inflation running hot. The reasoning is probably linked to the market wealth effect that many believe has underpinned US economic resilience. This is enough to suggest the dollar will not be the safe-haven of choice and may actually lag many other G10 currencies if stock market instability originates in tech/AI.
Still, contagion to broader US and world equity indices has so far been contained, while the Nasdaq drop has only erased the last 30 days of gains. AI-related sentiment will remain an input for FX this week, but could easily fade if tech stocks find some stability. From a macro perspective, despite the repricing lower in US rates, we do not feel this marks the start of a major USD downtrend. A December Fed hike remains a likely outcome; policymakers do not appear to be in a position to send a dovish message at the October meeting, and still-elevated energy prices argue against a material recovery in global bond markets.
A return to 101.0 in DXY remains possible over the coming weeks, but we do not see much more downside beyond that for now. The US calendar is rather light this week, while the FOMC is in its pre-meeting communication blackout. For now, we are not observing any obvious FX impact from souring US-Ukraine (and Europe) relationships. Markets are probably quite cautious about pricing in an imminent end to the Russia-Ukraine conflict or any longer-term implications for Europe. Things could change in the case of meaningful developments this week.
Francesco Pesole
EUR: French protests may curb upside for now
EUR/USD briefly dropped back below 1.120 overnight before inching higher again this morning. The move in short-term rate differentials has pushed our short-term fair value estimate for EUR/USD higher to around 1.137-1.139. The current undervaluation is therefore around 1.3-1.5%, broadly consistent with French fiscal risk remaining very much present, as reflected in the 10yr OAT-Bund spread hovering around 135-140bp.
Markets have appeared tentatively more relaxed about the budget situation. Still, continued widespread protests in France over the weekend should weigh on domestic stocks and could spill over into the bond market. We doubt that is enough to drive further sustained widening per se, but it may limit EUR/USD's ability to return to Friday's levels.
On the macro side, the highlight of the week is Friday's PMI release. Expectations are for a modest softening in the eurozone composite figure, while remaining well inside expansionary territory. Tomorrow, Germany's ZEW index will be in focus.
The balance of risks for EUR/USD is fairly even at this stage. Downside risk continues to stem from France, although it has abated somewhat as of late, while the upside comes from further AI concerns hitting Fed rate expectations. Our month-ahead target remains 1.130.
Francesco Pesole
CAD: Inflation still OK, a hike still possible
Canada releases inflation data for September today. The headline rate should accelerate at a 0.2% month-on-month pace, not particularly hot, especially given core measures have remained anchored around 2.0%.
The jobs market has given some warning signals, with two consecutive negative prints in August and September and the unemployment rate rising to 6.5%. Still, with growth proving resilient and a widening rate spread with the Fed, an (insurance) rate hike in December by the Bank of Canada remains a clear possibility. The BoC also releases its business outlook survey today.
Markets are fully pricing in a 25bp December hike, as well as 9bp for next week’s meeting. That suggests limited upside for the Canadian dollar, even if the October meeting is used to set the stage for a December move. That is, barring a surprise October hike, although we don’t sense that markets are underpricing here.
We don’t see much more downside for USD/CAD at this stage, with a return to 1.420 still our baseline for the month-end and year-end.
Francesco Pesole
CEE: Hungary to release its budget plan for the coming years
Today’s focus is Hungary’s draft budget for next year. Hungarian bonds have rallied strongly in recent weeks on growing expectations that the plan will target a deficit below 5% of GDP. However, much of the good news now appears priced in, creating downside risk if the government falls short of expectations. Even so, the broader outlook for bonds remains positive, particularly compared with this year’s 7.0-7.5% deficit, and we expect investors to buy any dip following a sell-off.
The region’s first economic releases arrive on Tuesday, with Polish wage, PPI and industrial production data. The main focus, however, will be the National Bank of Hungary meeting. We expect rates to remain unchanged at 5.50%, leaving attention on forward guidance. Although the central bank has identified the fiscal plan as a key factor for future easing, we believe cuts remain premature and, global conditions permitting, are unlikely before the end of this year or next year.
On Thursday, we expect the Central Bank of Turkey to resume its easing cycle for the first time since the US-Iran conflict began, cutting rates by 100bp to 36.00%. September’s inflation data provided a positive signal, while developments in investment funds point to downside risks for the economy in the final quarter. Although crowded long TRY positions offer less and less carry, they remain popular in emerging markets, and we expect this demand to persist in the coming months despite renewed rate cuts.
Beyond the scheduled events, we are monitoring political developments in Romania, where the new government appears highly likely to win a confidence vote. This should help stabilise EUR/RON after its decline late last week, and we expect the pair to settle around 5.340. In the Czech Republic, the Czech National Bank may offer its first signals ahead of the November meeting, when we expect another rate hike.
Frantisek Taborsky

articles.title: Rates Spark: Don’t expect a break back below 5%
articles.author: Padhraic Garvey, CFA
articles.fulltext:
We think the US 10yr stays above 5%, and in fact heads back up to 5.25%. That won't help the eurozone, which continues to grapple with the problem that is France. Probably overdone, but far from over
The mood for US Treasuries has calmed. But don't get too comfortable
Treasury market moves of late have been quite something. There were buyers in the 5.3% area post the CPI release on Wednesday. Then the Asian open coincided with some large falls in equities, with a particular focus on Korean equities, which prompted some follow-on buying of Treasuries. Note, however, that there have been decent buyers of Treasuries on an ongoing basis in the past number of weeks. It just has not translated into a meaningful move lower in yields, mostly as it had been offset by net shorts on Treasury futures. We've been overdue a reversal.
That said, we're not convinced this is a structural move, and we'd be quite surprised if we were to break below 5% on the 10yr yield. Treasuries did not react much to Thursday's data, but market participants will be aware that we had another good (low) jobless claims number, retail sales were firm and PPI inflation uncomfortably high. The market will likely use this as a platform from which to rebuild higher in yields over the weeks ahead, and into the mid-terms; especially with neither side voicing an intention to take action on the fiscal deficit. The issues of high printed inflation and a high deficit remain.
The balance of probabilities suggests there is at least one more leg of long-end weakness still to play out. This could take the US 10-year yield back into the 5.25% to 5.5% range. Other markets would likely move in tandem, mapping out similar, albeit less dramatic, blow-outs. With 5.25% looking like a mean-reversion level, we think the US 10-year yield could overshoot towards 5.5% and remain elevated for a number of months as bond market jitters persist. This could quite easily extend into the first quarter of 2027. Our views here are unchanged, despite recent moves.
The eurozone remains in the throes of an uneasy holding pattern at dodgy levels
The focus in the eurozone is increasingly insular, with France front and centre and setting the mood . Here too, there has been some market stability – but at uncomfortable levels. The standout move has been a doubling of the French 10yr swap spread from the 60bp area to the 120bp area. And French spreads to Germany are practically as wide as they've ever been since the dawn of the euro, even versus the immediate pre-EMU years. The safe narrative to reach for is the debt dynamics one, and the lack of ambition to correct it. Made worse, in fact, by the political options being offered for 2028.
This is probably overdone, as a swing to the right (should it occur) could have some tail positives that aren't currently properly discounted. Look at the improvement seen in Italian spreads following the rise of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. It's been gradual but persistent, and has not been overly impacted by French concerns. In that sense, the Italian response has been low beta in characterisation, which is good.
In fact, the first real bout of widening in French spreads can be traced back to President Emmanuel Macron's election gamble of mid-2024. Things subsequently calmed, but were not forgotten. The recent spike is an amplification and extension of an underlying tension that has not gone away. So, overdone? Probably, yes. But we also remain in a danger zone for bonds generally. Just like in the US, more overshoots to the upside are entirely foreseeable.

Author
Padhraic Garvey, CFA

articles.title: Asia FX Talking: More two-way risk emerging in USD/CNY
articles.author: Deepali Bhargava, Lynn Song, Chris Turner
articles.fulltext:
Higher Treasury yields and a broadly stronger dollar are starting to inject more two-way risk in USD/CNY, raising questions about whether it needs to drop much further. We suspect 6.67 will mark the lower end of this year's range. Korea's won remains well bid on the broadening export boom, while South Asia FX continues to struggle with high energy
USD/CNY: CNY might see a return of two-way risk ahead
USD/CNY has stabilised around the 6.70 level after briefly breaking below in September. The yuan’s gradual appreciation trajectory is expected to continue by many market participants.
Fundamental factors are starting to look more mixed. US-China yield spreads have widened to the highest levels on record. Foreign holdings of Chinese domestic assets have recovered this year, but FDI continues to contract. China continues to run a strong current account surplus, and exporters continue to sell into rallies.
For the rest of the year, USD/CNY may be relatively rangebound. Odds for a return of two-way volatility are increasing. Our 2026 forecast sees a fluctuation band of 6.67-6.92, with risks still balanced to the downside.
USD/KRW: Won holding up better than expected
The won is delivering quite the resilient performance. Yes, we did see the brief correction to 1390 on a hawkish Fed, but those USD gains have been quickly reversed. Our preference, however, remains for a 1325-1400 trading range into year-end given the difficult external environment. High US yields, some pick up in financial market volatility and stubbornly high energy prices all matter.
The local story remains encouraging. Consumer sentiment is picking up as the benefits of the chip export boom are broadening. Bank of Korea could hike 100bp over the next year.
Korean exporters now seem to have greater confidence in bringing money back to the won. Sub-1300 looks possible in 2027.
USD/INR: Higher rates not enough to lift the INR
The Reserve Bank of India has embarked on a rate hiking cycle, raising the repo rate by 25bp to 5.5%. Despite this, the rupee slipped against the dollar and continued to depreciate. Lack of a decisive tightening signal and a relatively neutral stance on rates likely triggered the response.
Absent a major upside inflation surprise from oil, El Niño-related food pressures, or a sharper INR depreciation, we expect the RBI to maintain a gradual tightening path, delivering another 50bp of hikes to a terminal repo rate of 6.0% by 2Q27.
After a brief surge in FII inflows, September saw around $6bn in outflows, driven by higher oil prices and a widening USD rate advantage. With limited near-term catalysts, the INR is likely to trade with a weaker bias.
USD/IDR: Renewed weakening pressures likely
Currency stability remains Bank Indonesia's primary objective. Rather than raising rates and increasing borrowing costs, BI appears willing to rely on targeted market measures to attract inflows and support the rupiah. This has helped IDR recover from its lows.
Although improving sentiment supported by greater policy certainty has eased near-term pressure on policymakers to hike rates, upside risks to inflation from higher fuel prices and a severe El Niño remain. We therefore continue to expect one 25bp rate hike in 2026.
Indonesia's external accounts remain a key source of vulnerability. FDI inflows are still subdued, FII inflows have weakened again, and the current account deficit is expected to widen, keeping depreciation pressures on the rupiah elevated. Meanwhile, declining FX reserves have reduced BI’s scope for sustained currency intervention.
USD/PHP: Potential breach of 63.0 driven by fundamentals
Elevated oil prices have intensified pressure on the oil-sensitive peso, making it one of the region’s worst-performing currencies year-to-date. The weakness reflects a deteriorating external position, with the current account deficit widening by roughly 50% to $15bn in 1H26 from a year earlier.
Inflation has reaccelerated above 7% YoY and remains persistently elevated, driven by food and fuel prices. Compared with regional peers, the Philippines stands out for its stronger pass-through of global oil prices into domestic fuel costs, amplifying inflationary pressures.
We expect the currency to remain under pressure as declining FX reserves limit the central bank's ability to intervene aggressively in the FX market, while weakening external fundamentals continue to weigh on investor sentiment.
USD/SGD: Likely to remain the strongest ASEAN currency
We continue to see upside risks to Singapore's inflation outlook, driven by resilient domestic demand and persistent price pressures across both goods and services. Underlying price dynamics point to further firming in core inflation over the coming months.
Persistent inflation risks from energy, food and domestic demand suggest the Monetary Authority of Singapore may not yet be finished tightening. As a result, we believe the October policy meeting remains a live event.
We expect modest policy tightening through a “very slight” increase in the slope of the SGD NEER policy band, potentially to around 1.5% annual appreciation. Such a move would provide additional support for the Singapore dollar amid an uncertain external environment.
USD/TWD: TWD weakens despite equity inflows and trade surplus
USD/TWD trended a little higher over the past month, trading within a range of 31.5-31.9 and partially unwinding the drop seen in August.
We’ve seen a mixed picture in terms of the Taiwan dollar’s key drivers. Yield spreads widened as the Fed hiked while the Central Bank of the Republic of China stayed on hold. There is also significant outflow pressure from Taiwan corporates investing abroad. However, equity market inflows generally continued over the past month, and Taiwan’s trade surplus continued to reach new highs.
With mixed drivers, further rangebound trading is expected in the near-term. The CBC continues to manage FX volatility, and we expect a rate hike at December’s meeting. Barring significant new catalysts, USD/TWD looks likely to stay within this year’s range of 31.2-32.5 through year-end.

articles.title: EMEA FX Talking: External headwinds up against local stories
articles.author: Rafal Benecki, Peter Virovacz, David Havrlant, Mateusz Sutowicz, Dmitry Dolgin, Muhammet Mercan, Chris Turner
articles.fulltext:
Like many emerging market currencies, those in the EMEA region have been hit by higher US Treasury yields and the stronger dollar. Yet the domestic stories look constructive for many, and a combination of some local rate hikes as well as light foreign positioning (ex Hungary) can insulate these currencies from the global bond market sell-off
EUR/PLN: Zloty swings with market sentiment
EUR/PLN has moved towards 4.40 after trading around the 4.30 level during summer. With market sentiment deteriorating amid geopolitical tensions in Iran, France and Russia, the coming weeks could challenge the zloty.
PLN has recently strengthened its correlation with EUR/USD, so the dollar’s future moves will be the key driver in the currency’s performance, while domestic factors are likely to take a back seat.
We retain a broadly positive stance on the zloty in the medium term due to solid GDP momentum and persistent outperformance. However, the balance of risks has become less favourable; the National Bank of Poland may deliver fewer hikes than priced, and a hot budget debate could reveal vulnerabilities.
EUR/HUF: A credibility boost is in the making for the forint
While EUR/HUF has shown some volatility recently, the swings have been far more moderate than we used to see. This reflects general positioning and the euro adoption story.
We think an idiosyncratic shock is coming with the 2027 budget and the mid-term fiscal consolidation plan. If the government delivers a credible plan, as we expect, and announces official talks on joining ERM II, this could provide a credibility boost to the forint.
A significant drop in the risk premium and some insulation from geopolitical market turbulence could take EUR/HUF down to the 350-355 area over the next month. This would, however, reopen the door to a National Bank of Hungary easing cycle starting in December, putting the HUF on a mild depreciation path over the following 12 months.
EUR/CZK: Braving the turbulence
The Czech Republic has also been affected by the global bond yield rally, with the turmoil applying depreciation pressure on the koruna. Inflation is set to increase on the back of rallying import prices and second-round effects of the oil price shock starting to bite.
We believe that equilibrium interest rates are higher than generally assumed, since the cost of capital must adjust to a world of protracted conflict and increased resource scarcity. A higher base rate is warranted to prevent the koruna from weakening further, which would exacerbate domestic price pressures.
That said, the ECB may turn more hesitant despite elevated inflation, as concerns over French fiscal issues rekindle fears of another euro crisis. In turn, the real interest rate differential should help the koruna withstand the turmoil and gradually appreciate once things have calmed down.
EUR/RON: Rating downgrade avoided, RON still vulnerable
EUR/RON had its second major move of the year, climbing from 5.28 to 5.35, which looks to be the near-term level. Official interventions have likely moderated the impact of significant outflow pressures through both September and so far in October – with the fear of rating downgrades and the protracted political instability as key drivers.
While the rating remained in place, the political arena is yet to find its consensus. The key positive element supporting the credit story remains the budget deficit, which stood at 2.89% of GDP as of August 2026 (vs 4.50% in August last year).
A tighter liquidity management has recently led FX implied yields to the highest levels since May 2025, although funding pressures have diminished from their early October peak. We expect the pair to remain around its current levels by year-end and close next year near 5.45.
EUR/RSD: RSD stable ahead of parliamentary elections
EUR/RSD has remained relatively flat in the range of 117.3–117.5. Yet again, the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has extended the operating waiver for Serbia's NIS refinery until 30 October. The NIS ownership issue is yet to be resolved.
Snap parliamentary elections have been called for 25 October, with President Aleksandar Vucic resigning in order to pursue premiership. The fiscal deficit has recently been revised higher, from 3.0% to 3.5% of GDP in 2026, mainly reflecting higher social expenditure.
At its October meeting, the National Bank of Serbia kept the key rate in place at 5.75%, continuing to highlight inflation uncertainty. Between January and August, the Bank sold €407m to keep the pair stable. We expect the pair to remain around the current levels ahead.
USD/UAH: NBU efforts to protect the UAH
The hryvnia remained under pressure as the dollar strengthened, partly due to renewed Middle East tensions. Consequently, USD/UAH temporarily broke above 45.0, reaching its highest level on record.
Hryvnia depreciation could have been sharper, but National Bank of Ukraine action provided support. In September, the central bank raised rates by 50bp to 16.0% and maintained sizeable FX interventions, with the four-week average near record highs.
The outlook for the hryvnia appears cloudy as the macroeconomic environment remains challenging – particularly as the ongoing war with Russia poses an increasing threat to the Ukrainian economy.
USD/KZT: Growing state FX sales backlog to boost KZT resilience
The tenge gained 5% against the US dollar in September, driven mainly by private capital inflows, particularly continued non-resident demand for KZT government bonds.
Combined net FX sales by the state oil fund (NFRK) and National Bank of Kazakhstan fell to zero in September, compared with $1.0–1.3bn per month in 1H26. As NFRK sales have remained below fiscal financing needs since mid-2026, an estimated $1.0–1.5bn backlog of FX sales has accumulated.
After gaining 25% YoY against USD, the tenge has limited upside, particularly amid global risk aversion and regional geopolitical uncertainty. At the same time, Kazakhstan’s high real rates should continue to attract carry-trade inflows, while the eventual release of the state FX sales backlog could ensure KZT resilience if market sentiment deteriorates.
USD/UZS: Still waiting for gold exports to catch up
After appreciating 1% against the US dollar in August, the soum was broadly flat in September and early October. This was slightly weaker than we expected, but still resilient given the global dollar rally and lower gold prices.
Gold exports remain a key variable for Uzbekistan’s FX market. There were no exports in August, and gold was exported only in April and July this year. Year-to-date volumes stand at just 18 mt, implying a substantial backlog compared with 85 mt in FY25 and the historical annual range of 80–120 mt.
Like Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan offers high real rates and is likely to continue doing so despite a potential monetary policy easing. As inflation has stabilised at 6.2–6.4% YoY, we see some room for a cautious cut from the current 14.00% policy rate before the end of the year.
USD/TRY: Rate cut expectations build as inflation eases
Fund volatility has not affected the dollarisation ratio. Net outflows in lira-denominated funds turned TRY625bn between the end of August and 6 October, excluding suspended funds. Meanwhile, outflows from FX-linked fund assets totalled $2.2bn, while higher TRY deposits and repo balances suggest dollarisation remains contained.
September’s CPI came in below consensus, supported by favourable food and transport. Annual CPI fell to 29.7% from 31.5% in August. Seasonally adjusted CPI, a key indicator closely monitored by the Central Bank of Turkey, slowed to 1.6% month-on-month from 2.2% in August, marking one of the lowest readings seen in recent years.
This backdrop increases the likelihood of a shift toward policy rate cuts. The recent investment fund disruption is likely to raise downside risks to activity. Given September’s CPI and weak domestic demand, we expect two 100bp cuts in October and December.
USD/ZAR: A resilient performance from the rand
The high-yield rand has been one of the better EM performers during the sell-off over the last month. Its fiscal metrics are not particularly great, (5% budget deficit, 80% debt to GDP), but the coalition government looks to be taking things in the right direction; a primary budget surplus is helpful here.
The South African Reserve Bank is helping out too, having hiked 25bp in September to 7.25%. It is threatening to hike rates again on a baseline view that core central banks hike another 50bp.
A difficult external environment suggests USD/ZAR may need to trade in a 16.00-16.60 range for the next three to six months. As 2027 progresses, however, the case for sub-16.00 levels builds.
USD/ILS: Israel’s higher credit rating provides a buffer
Israel’s high-quality credit rating (A-) has provided a buffer to the shekel during this debt crisis. That largely stems from Israel’s strong external investment position and relatively large domestic capital market. Additionally, the debt sell-off has yet to unhinge the US tech story – of which the shekel is a beneficiary.
In September, the Bank of Israel cut rates to 3.25%, citing low inflation. Markets currently price further aggressive cuts to the 2.00% area, which seems excessive. The BoI might prefer to save those rate cuts for when the dollar is broadly softer – maybe in 2Q27 – and when USD/ILS is threatening to run away sub-3.00.
Longer term, the trade-weighted ILS is very firm, and we suspect Israeli authorities will struggle to tolerate much further strength.

articles.title: FX Daily: Dollar holds gains as geopolitics heats up
articles.author: Chris Turner, Frantisek Taborsky, Francesco Pesole
articles.fulltext:
News over the weekend of continued Houthi strikes in Riyadh and a supposed 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine have had little meaningful impact on FX markets so far. The dollar remains well bid, and what could be a hot US September CPI this week will keep expectations of Fed tightening and a stronger dollar in play
USD: Geopolitics to keep the dollar supported
FX markets have been reasonably quiet at the start of the new week, barring a jump in the Indian rupee on some defensive measures instituted by the Reserve Bank of India. Energy prices do not quite know what to make of weekend developments, where Houthi strikes against Saudi Arabia have escalated local tensions, while at the same time US President Donald Trump has tried to present an 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine. On the latter, Russia has yet to respond to the invite and continues to target energy infrastructure in Ukraine.
Instead, FX markets are preferring to concentrate on the cyclical story of decent US growth, above-target inflation and the prospect of the Federal Reserve hiking 75bp from current levels. Barring a big fall in energy prices this week, which seems unlikely, Wednesday's release of September US CPI inflation looks set to keep those Fed tightening expectations broadly intact. Our team see upside risks to the consensus of 0.2% month-on-month on the core reading. And as James Smith discusses in his weekly column , it may not be until next spring when tightening expectations can drop out of money markets. This points to the dollar staying supported by the cyclical story for a good while yet.
Other highlights this week include a new World Economic Outlook from the IMF and the US 3Q earnings season kicking off tomorrow when bulge bracket banks release.
With US bond markets closed for the Columbus Day public holiday, it should be a quiet day for FX markets. But DXY consolidation above 102 looks bullish, and our preference would be for a push up to 102.85 this week.
Chris Turner
EUR: Little reprieve for the euro
EUR/USD is consolidating near 1.12, and support remains fragile. French debt spreads remain near their widest, with Marine Le Pen's counter-budget proposal last week raising more questions than it answered. In theory, the French government's budget proposal of €43bn in new savings will be debated in parliament this week. Consensus seems to expect that this will make little progress, but that the government might ultimately be able to pass this budget by decree. Here, protagonists in parliament might avoid trying to bring down the government, which would make the French debt crisis worse than it already is. This is hardly a euro positive, however.
Speculators and the FX options market remain quite bearish on EUR/USD currently, although positioning is starting to get a little stretched. But barring a big US policy misstep, which again questions investors' long dollar exposure, the macro story remains EUR/USD bearish. For the near term, a further dip towards 1.1100/1120 looks more likely.
Chris Turner
CHF: Caught between higher rates and France
EUR/CHF is consolidating after its heavy fall just over a week ago. That move was driven by French debt problems being severe enough to curtail European Central Bank tightening expectations. However, it is not clear that short-dated euro rates need to fall a lot further from here, unless we see a sharp drop in energy prices. Currently, the market prices 22bp of hikes in December (we look for a 25bp hike) and then a further 30-40bp of tightening into next year. With eurozone inflation still pushing higher (September eurozone CPI should be confirmed at 3.8% year-on-year this week), it seems too early to expect 2027 hikes from the ECB to be cancelled.
This all adds up to a mixed picture for EUR/CHF. We cannot rule out a correction to the 0.9230/50 area should the OAT-Bund spread decisively push through the 150bp area, but any brief periods of calm can see EUR/CHF trade back up to 0.9350/9400.
Chris Turner
CEE: Inflation tests meet global FX headwinds
This week’s focus is on regional inflation releases and speakers. Romania’s September inflation is due tomorrow; we expect it to rise from 6.2% to 6.4% and, consistent with the central bank’s guidance last week, increase further through year-end. In the Czech Republic, final data should confirm September inflation at 2.5%, while Czech National Bank core inflation is likely to edge up from 3.0% to 3.1-3.2%, above the central bank’s forecast. Poland’s headline inflation should be confirmed at 4.0% on Wednesday, followed by a likely drop in core inflation from 3.3% to 3.1% on Thursday, giving the National Bank of Poland more room to manoeuvre. Hungary releases wage data on Friday; wage growth remains high relative to the region and continues to pose inflationary risks.
Beyond the data calendar, attention will turn to the IMF meetings in Bangkok, where CEE officials are expected to speak. Hungary may publish next year’s draft budget and medium-term fiscal outlook late in the week. Market expectations have moved from around 5.5% towards 5.0%; although this raises the bar for a positive surprise, the direction remains supportive for bonds. In Romania, talks on forming a new government continue. Signs of progress emerged late last week and should help stabilise EUR/RON.
CEE FX remains primarily driven by global factors, and our bearish regional bias is broadly unchanged. After the NBP meeting, EUR/PLN rose into our expected 4.380-4.400 range and is likely to stay near its upper end in the coming days. The forint is awaiting the government’s 2027 budget announcement but remains exposed to higher energy prices and a stronger US dollar. The koruna remains the outlier, supported by a wider interest-rate differential. We retain a bullish koruna view and expect EUR/CZK to move towards 24.250.
Frantisek Taborsky

articles.title: Rates Spark: Don’t get too comfortable
articles.author: Padhraic Garvey, CFA, Benjamin Schroeder
articles.fulltext:
US Treasuries have calmed. But plenty of opportunity and time for markets to (re-)change their tune. Italian bond investors signalled their liking of an electoral reform that would potentially improve governability. We draw the parallel with France, where improved governability is a prerequisite for a material tightening of spreads
Treasuries sail calmer waters, but we'd not get too comfortable
It's been a good week for US bond auctions. Solid 10yr and 30yr auctions over consecutive days show there is a level where buyers step in. The 30yr auction saw a strong international and domestic bid that took down the paper at secondary market levels, and the previous day's 10yr auction came a tad rich to secondary. The 10yr yield is back below 5.25%, partly a reflection of this, but also reflective of some value hunters generally. It does not mean the bond market sell-off is over, but it does at least put it on pause, at least just for now.
We also note that Treasuries are holding on to the moderate richness built since the increased long-end-buyback announcement, in the guise of tighter swap spreads; the antithesis of what we saw in France over the past weeks, where swap spreads gapped wider by a factor of at least two. Nothing like that has occurred in the US, as the 10yr yield holds at just under a 40bp spread to 10yr SOFR.
That said, the 10yr swap spread is off its recent lows, and we continue to anticipate a likely widening in US swap spreads ahead as we head into the mid-terms with not nearly enough chat on fiscal deficit-reduction actions plans. Plenty of opportunity for markets to wake up and decide to start to price that through a widening in the implied Treasury credit spread to the SOFR risk-free rate.
Italy highlights the importance of governability
Thursday saw a recovery in European government bond spreads that was led by Italian bonds. Their 10y spread over Bunds tightened around 5bp towards 110bp. This is still above the levels seen before French repricing started to spill over, but it came with a backdrop of rising energy prices. Since February, higher oil prices have tended to generally widen spreads and in particular hurt Italian bonds relatively more.
The outperformance was attributed to the Italian PM Meloni securing the final vote for her electoral reform that would grant any leading coalition with more than 42% of the votes bonus seats to secure stable majorities. It is actually unclear whether she will benefit from this, but the prospect of clearer majorities and better governability is in general a positive for anyone looking for exposure to sovereign risk.
It also highlights what we see as a precondition for any lasting recovery in French bond spreads – political predictability and stability. With the two rounds of the presidential elections only in April and May next year, French bond spreads are still looking at more than half a year of higher volatility and continued spread elevation.
Friday’s events and market view
It will be another relatively quiet day in terms of macro releases. The only notable data release is the University of Michigan US consumer confidence index. More attention may fall on central bank communication. The ECB’s Lagarde will join the Ecofin meeting, and public appearances are scheduled for Wunsch, Cipollone and Schnabel.
After markets close, eyes will be out for possible rating updates. Among the scheduled reviews are of Belgium (Moody’s A1/Stable) and the UK (S&P AA/Stable).

articles.title: Rates Spark: Bifurcated risk sentiment
articles.author: Michiel Tukker, Benjamin Schroeder
articles.fulltext:
Risk sentiment is improving as equities rise, oil trends lower and volatility eases, but financial conditions remain uneven. Marine Le Pen’s fiscal plan may briefly support OATs, but a lack of credibility and the election uncertainty ahead still point to spread widening risks
Big contrasts in financial condition measures
Risk sentiment is turning more optimistic again, at least for now, with French government spreads tightening and the S&P 500 at new highs. Meanwhile, Brent oil temporarily nudged below $100, helping to ease market concerns about inflation. Implied rate volatility has also ticked slightly lower, suggesting markets are hoping the worst is behind us. But the overall macro landscape continues to be strained by many, often opposing, forces, and therefore we doubt rates will calmly settle at current levels.
One could argue that financial conditions are looking good at a macro level, but not everyone will agree. Financial conditions based on record equities and still relatively tight credit spreads suggest a very positive market outlook. But consumers needing to refinance a mortgage are unlikely to agree. The same parallel can be drawn with European governments. Unless growth expectations for the eurozone continue to improve, AI-related or otherwise, concerns about European government debt can continue to be a disrupting force in markets.
Le Pen’s fiscal plan likely offers OAT spreads only temporary relief
Presidential race front-runner Marine Le Pen outlined her fiscal consolidation plans, which have been well received by markets. French bond spreads liked what they heard and the 10y OAT/Bund spread tightened almost 10bp towards 125bp. While acknowledging the scale of France's fiscal challenges, on closer inspection we think the plan relies on overly optimistic assumptions and difficult-to-deliver measures, limiting the scope for lasting spread compression.
On the positive side in the near term, it could also signal less resistance to the government’s current proposal for 2027, which targets a deficit of 5% rather than the 3.7% that Le Pen’s plan envisages. Looking ahead to the elections, we still face a prolonged period of uncertainty and headline risks that is likely to deter investors from exposure to French debt, and the plans might even expose her presidential campaign to more attacks from her opponents.
More importantly, we think that she will also face the same public resistance to her plans as have most other efforts to rein in spending. Currently, student unrest across the country is filling the headlines and, on Tuesday, unions called for nationwide strikes in early November.
While hitting the right tone, we don’t see lasting relief for spreads from plans that are difficult to deliver on. On balance, we still see risks tilted towards a re-widening of spreads as we head closer to the elections and expect the spread to remain in the 125-150bp range for now rather than move lastingly lower.
Wednesday’s events and market view
The day will be light on data with the highlights being German industrial production and the US consumer credit data. However, we will see a few European Central Bank officials speaking, such as Piero Cipollone and Boris Vujcic, and in the US, the Federal Reserve will release the minutes of the September FOMC meeting.
In primary markets, Germany will auction a new 7y Bund (€4bn) while the UK tenders 2y and 5y gilts (£2.5bn). The US then auctions 10y notes (US$39bn).

articles.title: EUR Money Markets: Tightening as intended
articles.author: Benjamin Schroeder
articles.fulltext:
The ECB hike discount is stretched, but hard to lean against given the high level of uncertainty. Liquidity conditions will continue to tighten. Repo markets should absorb the adjustment, but a higher reserve requirement, year-end pressures or ECB borrowing stigma could still trigger a sharper rise in money-market rates
ECB pricing is looking increasingly stretched
The European Central Bank faces a challenging backdrop of renewed energy market stress alongside surprisingly resilient economic growth, as reflected in the latest flash PMIs. This mix has pushed short-end rates to price in a tightening cycle that sees three to four more hikes over the next year. We think this is too much and expect only one more hike from the ECB, taking the deposit facility rate to 2.75%. But we have to acknowledge that this outlook largely hinges on the assumption that geopolitical tensions will start to ease after the US mid-term elections.
Liquidity conditions tighten and approaching critical thresholds
Money markets face progressively tighter liquidity conditions as the ECB continues to shrink its balance sheet and transitions to a new operational framework for implementing monetary policy. The new framework, introduced in 2024, aims to nudge banks into a more active role, using liquidity operations as part of the ECB's day-to-day liquidity management. The ideal is a self-balancing system where banks decide how much liquidity they need while the ECB continues to offer unlimited liquidity at a fixed rate.
By design, as excess liquidity continues to decline, short-term rates are expected to rise. The indicator the ECB appears to watch closely is the repo market. Officials have indicated that repo rates moving toward the rate charged on the ECB’s one-week main refinancing operations (MROs) would be consistent with the framework functioning as intended, since banks would increasingly have economic incentives to substitute market funding with ECB refinancing operations.
At a later stage, the ECB plans to introduce both structural refinancing operations and a structural bond portfolio aimed at supplying a baseline level of reserves. The objective is to cover the structural liquidity demand arising from reserve requirements and autonomous liquidity factors such as banknotes in circulation.
One issue that the ECB has not yet solved is that funding via the ECB comes with a perceived stigma. That is what could lead to a more noticeable squeeze higher in money market rates.
Excess liquidity is at €2.12tr at the moment. Current estimates suggest banks may wish to operate with somewhere between €1.5tr and €2tr of excess liquidity, although uncertainty remains substantial because observed reserve demand under the new framework is untested. The estimates hinge on assumptions around liquidity coverage ratios that banks want to maintain and the share of reserves within the portfolios of high-quality liquid assets backing those ratios. Nevertheless, these estimates suggest that repo funding rates could begin to rise more noticeably from late 2026 into 2027. Banks with relatively smaller liquidity buffers or less active access to repo markets may experience funding pressures earlier than the system-wide aggregates would suggest.
While we think there is only a low probability of it happening, the process could accelerate if the ECB follows through with proposals to increase the minimum reserve requirement from 1% to 2%. This would immediately absorb roughly €176bn of liquidity from the banking system. The rationale is to lower the ECB’s losses stemming from paying interest on the liquidity created by the bond-buying programmes. Reuters reported in July on alternative options, such as not paying interest to banks on some of their excess reserves, ie applying a tiered rate, or even charging fees.
Banks aren't yet feeling the pressure to go to the ECB for liquidity
Funding markets tighten as they take over liquidity redistribution
We are already seeing the €STR unsecured overnight benchmark drift higher, but it still stands 6bp below the deposit facility rate. If we take the latest ECB Survey of Monetary Analysts conducted ahead of the September ECB meeting at face value, then €STR should stabilise around 5bp below the deposit facility rate. Since €STR is not a pure interbank rate, but rather reflects wholesale unsecured borrowing by banks from a broader set of financial counterparties, a negative spread relative to the deposit facility rate can persist as these counterparties do not have direct access to ECB facilities.
Further out the funding curve, we see the 6m Euribor/€STR-OIS spread implying banks are willing to take on unsecured term funding slightly above the implied MRO rate, which sits 15bp above the deposit facility rate: 6m Euribor/€STR-OIS is at 29bp, while the MRO rate is 21bp above €STR.
To be fair, they are not perfect substitutes. Euribor is unsecured whereas MRO borrowing is collateralised. However, the persistence of a positive spread also suggests that banks continue to attach some value to avoiding direct recourse to ECB funding.
Overnight repo rates have continued to drift very gradually higher over the past months and are now largely above, but still close to, the ECB’s deposit facility rate.
Funding rates continue to gradually drift higher
At the same time, repo market activity has increased materially. Volumes captured by benchmarks such as the STOXX GC Pooling overnight index are already close to levels last seen in 2014, before the asset purchase programmes began injecting substantial liquidity into the banking system. This suggests that liquidity redistribution in money markets is becoming increasingly important as excess liquidity declines, consistent with the ECB's objective of encouraging a more active role for market-based intermediation.
Note that, looking further out to 1y, term GC rates against German and Italian government collateral remain below the implied MRO rate. This suggests market participants still expect liquidity redistribution through private markets to remain sufficient, without widespread recourse to ECB refinancing operations.
Money market secured and unsecured curves versus OIS
The upcoming year-end will provide another important test of liquidity conditions, as balance-sheet constraints typically reduce market-making capacity and increase funding demand. Funding markets may face additional pressure precisely as concerns surrounding European sovereign debt sustainability have re-emerged.
In particular, elevated political uncertainty in France raises the possibility that sovereign-bank linkages receive greater market attention. While French GC curves have only widened modestly so far, government bond spreads have reached their widest levels since 2012. At this stage, markets appear to be pricing in political uncertainty rather than fundamental default risk. Five-year French CDS spreads have risen sharply but remain below the levels observed during the 2017 Frexit episode.
Liquidity conditions are likely to continue tightening as QT steadily reduces excess reserves in the banking system. The base case remains an orderly tightening, with the repo market absorbing redistribution and repo clearing moving toward the MRO rate. The risk of a disorderly squeeze is most acute if the minimum reserve requirement is raised simultaneously with continued QT, or if a bank-specific liquidity event forces recourse to ECB facilities and triggers stigma-related contagion.

articles.title: GBP Money Markets: High premium for terming out
articles.author: Michiel Tukker
articles.fulltext:
Markets are pricing in more than four Bank of England hikes as oil trades around $100, but we think expectations have turned too hawkish, offering value further out the sterling money market curve. Meanwhile, ample reserves mean any material liquidity repricing remains a medium-term risk
Term risk premium offers opportunities
Sterling money market rates have shown significant swings on the back of oil price moves, and we should brace for more volatility. For every $10 increase in oil prices, the 2yr gilt yield rises by around 15bp. With Brent oil at $100, markets are pricing in more than four hikes from the Bank of England over the coming year. This would bring SONIA to around 4.75%.
We think markets have turned too hawkish on the Bank of England and therefore see value further out the money market curve. Trading this market is difficult, however, as any further escalation in the Middle East would immediately push interest rates higher again. For this reason, we believe the curve embeds a significant risk premium for longer-maturity exposures.
Our economist does not expect the BoE to hike rates, and the central bank’s communication is also more dovish than market pricing. Second-round inflation risks are limited, as the labour market has already cooled significantly over the past year. At 3.75%, we believe the policy rate is already restricting the economy, limiting the risk of overheating. As inflation should converge to target by mid-2027, we see scope for the BoE to cut rates towards 3.25%.
Markets are significantly more hawkish than economists
Liquidity costs still to rise, but not immediately
Even though SONIA rates seem to have stabilised at 2bp below Bank Rate, we still think liquidity could become more expensive in future. Quantitative tightening continues to withdraw reserves from the system, and banks increasingly rely on the Bank of England’s liquidity facilities. The Short-Term Repo (STR) facility, which provides one-week reserves, is priced at Bank Rate and requires high-quality collateral, mainly gilts. The pricing of the six-month Indexed Long-Term Repo (ILTR) facility is more complex and increases as demand for reserves rises.
SONIA has settled around 2bp below Bank Rate, but could still drift higher
When demand at the ILTR auctions exceeds £8bn, banks will have to pay more for their funding, increasing liquidity costs. In July, the maximum allocation was £7.4bn, close to the threshold. Below the threshold, the spread paid by banks is fixed between 3bp and 15bp, depending on the quality of collateral. Above the £8bn threshold, the Bank of England will charge higher spreads, although the exact calculation is not public. The maximum allocation is set at £35bn, which offers plenty of headroom for the coming years.
Reserves are more costly when demand for ILTR exceeds £8bn
The Bank of England expects the clearing spread for the lowest-quality collateral to settle around 20-40bp, well above the minimum spread of 15bp. In effect, this would increase overall liquidity costs in sterling markets. Consequently, SONIA could still drift higher, potentially above Bank Rate. That said, SONIA is an overnight rate, while the ILTR facility provides six-month liquidity. SONIA also focuses on wholesale deposits from non-banks and therefore captures a different market segment from banks with access to the BoE’s facilities. As such, the pass-through will not be one-to-one.
The good news is that reserves remain ample and we are still far from a significant repricing of liquidity. Banks are unlikely to bid above the minimum clearing spreads for now, so allocations will likely remain capped at £8bn. Only once the allocation hits the threshold for multiple consecutive weeks would we start to anticipate a material drift higher in SONIA and other liquidity measures.
